metadata.title: Accelerated dynamics with dry friction via time scaling and averaging of doubly nonlinear evolution equations

items.name: Lemma A.1
items.statement: Let $a: [s_0, +\infty[ \to \mathbb{R}$ be a positive real valued function which verifies $\lim_{u \to +\infty} a(u) = 0$. Take $\alpha > 1$. Then $\lim_{s \to +\infty} A(s) = 0$, where $$A (s) = \frac {1}{s ^ {\alpha - 1}} \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} u ^ {\alpha - 2} a (u) d u.$$
items.proof: Given $\epsilon > 0$, let us take $T_{\epsilon}$ such that $s_0 < T_{\epsilon}$ and $a(u) \leq \epsilon$ for $t \geq T_{\epsilon}$. For $s > T_{\epsilon}$, let us write $$\begin{aligned} A (s) &= \frac {1}{s ^ {\alpha - 1}} \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {T _ {\epsilon}} u ^ {\alpha - 2} a (u) d u + \frac {1}{s ^ {\alpha - 1}} \int_ {T _ {\epsilon}} ^ {s} u ^ {\alpha - 2} a (u) d u \\ &\leq \frac {1}{s ^ {\alpha - 1}} \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {T _ {\epsilon}} u ^ {\alpha - 2} a (u) d u + \frac {\epsilon}{\alpha - 1}. \\ \end{aligned}$$ Letting $s$ go to $+\infty$, we obtain $$\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {s \to + \infty} A (s) \leq \frac {\epsilon}{\alpha - 1}.$$ This being true for any $\epsilon > 0$, we infer that $\lim_{s \to +\infty} A(s) = 0$ [Since $age0$, also $A(s)ge0$; hence $0leliminf Alelimsup Aleepsilon/(alpha-1)$ for every $epsilon>0$.], which gives the claim.
items.remark: [Prove hint: split the weighted integral at $T_epsilon$ and use nonnegativity to obtain the missing lower bound $A(s)ge0$.]

items.name: Convex subdifferential
items.statement: For a convex function $F:mathcal H	omathbb Rcup{+infty}$, its subdifferential at $xinoperatorname{dom}F$ is $partial F(x):={uinmathcal H: F(y)ge F(x)+langle u,y-xangle 	ext{for every }yinmathcal H}$.

items.statement: $$\phi : \mathcal {H} \rightarrow \mathbb {R} \text { satisfies } \phi (x) = r \| x \| \text { for some } r > 0.\tag {1.2}$$

items.name: Fenchel conjugate
items.statement: For $f:mathcal H	omathbb Rcup{+infty}$, its Legendre--Fenchel conjugate is $f^*(g):=sup_{xinmathcal H}{langle g,xangle-f(x)}$.
items.remark: [Notation: the paper writes $f^*$; conjugacy gives $ginpartial f(x)iff xinpartial f^*(g)$ under the stated proper convex lsc hypotheses.]

items.name: Closed ball and distance to the ball
items.statement: For $r>0$, $mathbb B(0,r):={uinmathcal H:|u|le r}$ and $operatorname{dist}(x,mathbb B(0,r)):=inf_{binmathbb B(0,r)}|x-b|$. For this closed convex ball, $operatorname{proj}_{mathbb B(0,r)}(x)$ denotes its unique metric projection.
items.remark: [Foundation: Foundation.Projection.BestApproximation] recall isChebyshev_of_nonempty_isClosed_convex; projection is unique and continuous.

items.name: Theorem 2.1
items.statement:
Let $z:[t_0, +\infty [\rightarrow \mathcal{H}$ be a global solution trajectory of (DRYGRAD). Then, $t\mapsto f(z(t))$ is a decreasing function, and the following properties are satisfied

(i) $\int_{t_0}^{+\infty}\| \dot{z} (t)\| ^2 dt < +\infty ;$
(ii) $\int_{t_0}^{+\infty}\| \dot{z} (t)\| dt < +\infty ;$
(iii) the trajectory $t \mapsto z(t)$ converges strongly as $t \to +\infty$, and its limit $z_{\infty}$ satisfies $$\| \nabla f (z _ {\infty}) \| = r.$$
(iv) Either the trajectory stabilizes in finite time at $z_{\infty}$ such that $\| \nabla f(z_{\infty}) \| = r$, which is the general case, or else the trajectory satisfies for all $t \geq t_0$ the inequality $\| \nabla f(z(t)) \| > r$.
items.proof:
(i) and (ii) Take the scalar product of (DRYGRAD) with $\dot{z}(t)$. We get $$\| \dot {z} (t) \| ^ {2} + \langle \partial \phi (\dot {z} (t)), \dot {z} (t) angle +  rac {d}{d t} f (z (t)) = 0. 	ag {2.3}$$ According to the properties of a dry friction potential we have $$0 = \phi (0) \geq \phi (\dot {z} (t)) + \langle \partial \phi (\dot {z} (t)), - \dot {z} (t) angle$$ which gives $$\langle \partial \phi (\dot {z} (t)), \dot {z} (t) angle \geq \phi (\dot {z} (t)) \geq r \| \dot {z} (t) \|.$$ Combining the above property with $(2.3)$ we obtain $$\| \dot {z} (t) \| ^ {2} + r \| \dot {z} (t) \| +  rac {d}{d t} f (z (t)) \leq 0. 	ag {2.4}$$ Therefore $ rac{d}{dt} f(z(t)) \leq 0$, which gives that $t \mapsto f(z(t))$ is a nonincreasing function. Integrating (2.4), and using the fact that $f$ is bounded from below gives the integral estimates (i) and (ii). [Indeed, for $T>t_0$, integration yields $int_{t_0}^T(|dot z|^2+r|dot z|)dtle f(z(t_0))-f(z(T))le f(z(t_0))-inf_{mathcal H}f$; let $T	oinfty$ and use $r>0$.]

(iii) Let us now come to the convergence properties of the solution trajectories of (DRYGRAD). Since $\int_{t_0}^{+\infty}\| \dot{z} (t)\| dt < +\infty$, it is immediate to verify that $z(t)$ satisfies the Cauchy property, and therefore converges strongly as $t	o +\infty$. [For $t_2ge t_1$, $|z(t_2)-z(t_1)|leint_{t_1}^{t_2}|dot z(u)|du$, and the right-hand side tends to $0$ as $t_1,t_2	oinfty$; completeness of $mathcal H$ supplies the limit.] Let us call $z_{\infty}$ its limit. Since $
abla f$ is continuous we have that, as $tightarrow +\infty$ $$
abla f (z (t)) 	o 
abla f (z _ {\infty}).$$ From the equivalent formulation of (DRYGRAD) $$\dot {z} (t) = (I + \partial \phi) ^ {- 1} (- 
abla f (z (t)))$$ and the continuity of the resolvent operator we get $$\lim _ {t 	o + \infty} \dot {z} (t) = (I + \partial \phi) ^ {- 1} (- 
abla f (z _ {\infty})).$$ Since $\int_{t_0}^{+\infty}\| \dot{z} (t)\| dt < +\infty$ we deduce that $\lim_{t	o +\infty}\dot{z} (t) = 0$ [The preceding resolvent formula already shows that $dot z(t)$ has a limit; an $L^1$ function with a finite limit must have limit $0$, since a nonzero limit would give an infinite tail integral.] and $$(I + \partial \phi) ^ {- 1} (- 
abla f (z _ {\infty})) = 0.$$ By definition of $\phi$, this gives $\| 
abla f(z_{\infty}) \| \leq r$.

(iv) Let us now show that $\|
abla f(z_{\infty})\|=r$, and examine the finite time convergence property. We have proved that the trajectory $t\mapsto z(t)$ converges strongly as $t	o+\infty$ to a limit $z_{\infty}$, and that $\|
abla f(z_{\infty})\|\leq r$. There are two different cases to examine: (a) The trajectory $t \mapsto z(t)$ satisfies for all $t \geq t_0$ $$\| 
abla f (z (t)) \| > r.$$ Then at the limit we have $\| 
abla f(z_{\infty})\| = r$ [for if the limit were $<r$, continuity would give $|
abla f(z(t))|<r$ for all sufficiently large $t$, contradicting case (a).], and the trajectory $z(\cdot)$ reaches $z_{\infty}$ after an infinite time. (b) There exists a finite time $t_1 > t_0$ such that $$\| 
abla f (z (t _ {1})) \| = r.$$ Indeed at time $t_{1}$ the vector field which governs the dynamic is equal to zero, which by Cauchy--Lipschitz formula implies that the trajectory remains fixed at this point. [More explicitly, the soft-threshold vector field is $F(z)=
abla f(z)-operatorname{proj}_{mathbb B(0,r)}
abla f(z)$; $|
abla f(z(t_1))|=r$ implies $F(z(t_1))=0$, so the constant solution has the same Cauchy data and uniqueness identifies it with $z$.] So we have finite convergence. Thus, in all cases we have at the limit that $\|
abla f(z_{\infty})\| = r$. ■

items.name: Theorem 3.1
items.proof:
(i) Let us use the specific form of the dry friction potential $\phi$. As long as $\dot{z}(t) 
eq 0$, we have $$\dot {z} (t) + r  rac {\dot {z} (t)}{\| \dot {z} (t) \|} + 
abla f (z (t)) = 0. 	ag {3.1}$$ After derivation of (3.1) with respect to $t$, we get $$\ddot {z} (t) + r  rac {\ddot {z} (t)}{\| \dot {z} (t) \|} - r \dot {z} (t)  rac {1}{\| \dot {z} (t) \| ^ {2}}  rac {d}{d t} (\| \dot {z} (t) \|) + 
abla^ {2} f (z (t)) \dot {z} (t) = 0. 	ag {3.2}$$ Taking the scalar product with $\dot{z}(t)$ we get $$\left(1 +  rac {r}{\| \dot {z} (t) \|}ight) \langle \ddot {z} (t), \dot {z} (t) angle - r  rac {d}{d t} (\| \dot {z} (t) \|) + \left\langle 
abla^ {2} f (z (t)) \dot {z} (t), \dot {z} (t) ightangle = 0. 	ag {3.3}$$ According to the convexity of $f$ we get [At points of twice differentiability, convexity gives $langle
abla^2f(z(t))dot z(t),dot z(t)anglege0$; moreover $langleddot z,dot zangle= rac12 rac d{dt}|dot z|^2$.] $$ rac {1}{2} \left(1 +  rac {r}{\| \dot {z} (t) \|}ight)  rac {d}{d t} (\| \dot {z} (t) \| ^ {2}) - r  rac {d}{d t} (\| \dot {z} (t) \|) \leq 0. 	ag {3.4}$$ Equivalently $\| \dot {z} (t) \|  rac {d}{d t} (\| \dot {z} (t) \|) \leq 0, [Indeed, expand the preceding left-hand side: $ rac12(1+r/|dot z|) rac d{dt}|dot z|^2-r rac d{dt}|dot z|=|dot z| rac d{dt}|dot z|$.] 	ag {3.5}$$ which gives $ rac{d}{dt}\left(\|\dot{z}(t)\|ight) \leq 0$. Therefore $t \mapsto \| \dot{z}(t) \|$ is decreasing.

(ii) According to (ii) in Theorem 2.1, and $t \mapsto \| \dot{z}(t) \|$ is decreasing, we deduce that for all $t \geq t_0$ $$(t - t _ {0}) \| \dot {z} (t) \| \leq \int_ {t _ {0}} ^ {t} \| \dot {z} (u) \| d u \leq \int_ {t _ {0}} ^ {+ \infty} \| \dot {z} (u) \| d u <   + \infty$$ which gives, that for some positive constant $C$ $$\| \dot {z} (t) \| \leq  rac {C}{t}.$$ Indeed we have $\| \dot {z} (t) \| = o \left( rac {1}{t}ight)$ thanks to the following lemma [The hypotheses hold because (i) gives monotonicity and Theorem 2.1(ii) gives integrability; Lemma 3.1 yields $t|dot z(t)|	o0$.] (apply it with $h(t) = \|\dot{z}(t)\|$ ).
items.remark:
[Prove hint: differentiate only on intervals where $dot z
e0$; convexity makes the Hessian quadratic form nonnegative.]

items.name: Time scaling and weighted averaging
items.statement: Given an increasing $C^1$ map $	au$ and a trajectory $z$, set $y(s):=z(	au(s))$. Given $y$, define its averaged trajectory $x$ by $dot x(s)+dot	au(s)^{-1}(x(s)-y(s))=0$ and $x(s_0)=y(s_0)$. For $	au(s)=s^2/(2(alpha-1))$, this is $sdot x(s)+(alpha-1)x(s)=(alpha-1)y(s)$.
items.remark: [Notation: this is the paper's time-scaling/averaging construction; differentiate only where the stated trajectories have the required regularity.]

items.name: Bregman distance generated by a differentiable convex function
items.statement:
If $F$ is differentiable and convex, its Bregman distance is $D_F(a,b):=F(b)-F(a)-langle
abla F(a),b-aangle$. In (3.10), $D(g(t),g_infty)=D_{f^*}(g(t),g_infty)$.
items.remark: [Note: the formula requires $f^*$ to be differentiable along the trajectory; otherwise formulate it with a chosen subgradient.]

items.name: Dual potential and Bregman distance
items.statement:
$$\psi(v):=\phi(v)+\frac{1}{2}\|v\|^{2},\qquad \psi^ {*} (\xi) = \frac {1}{2} \mathrm{dist} ^ {2} (\xi , \mathbb {B} (0, r)),$$
$$D (g (t), g _ {\infty}) = f ^ {*} (g _ {\infty}) - f ^ {*} (g (t)) - \left\langle \nabla f ^ {*} (g (t)), g _ {\infty} - g (t) \right\rangle . \tag {3.10}$$
items.remark: [Foundation: Foundation.Projection.BestApproximation] recall metric projection facts | [Note: differentiability of $f^*$ is needed for the displayed Bregman formula.]

items.name: Theorem 3.2
items.statement:
Let $z: [t_0, +\infty[ 	o \mathcal{H}$ be a global solution trajectory of (DRYGRAD). Then $g(t) := 
abla f(z(t))$ is a solution trajectory of the generalized Riemannian gradient flow $$ rac {d}{d t} \left(\partial f ^ {*} (g (t))ight) + g (t) - p r o j _ {\mathbb {B} (0, r)} (g (t)) 
i 0. 	ag {3.9}$$ The following convergence properties are satisfied: (i) $t \mapsto dist^2(
abla f(z(t)), \mathbb{B}(0, r))$ is a decreasing function, and, as $t 	o +\infty$, $$d i s t (
abla f (z (t)), \mathbb {B} (0, r)) = o \left( rac {1}{\sqrt {t}}ight);$$ (ii) For any $g_{\infty} \in \mathbb{B}(0, r)$, the function $t \mapsto D(g(t), g_{\infty})$ is decreasing where $$D (g (t), g _ {\infty}) = f ^ {*} (g _ {\infty}) - f ^ {*} (g (t)) - \left\langle 
abla f ^ {*} (g (t)), g _ {\infty} - g (t) ightangle . 	ag {3.10}$$
items.proof:
The dissipative properties associated with the above Riemannian gradient flow are obtained by using the Bregman distance defined by $(3.10)$. By deriving this expression we get $$ egin{aligned}  rac {d}{d t} D (g (t), g _ {\infty}) &= -  rac {d}{d t} (f ^ {*} (g (t))) - \left\langle  rac {d}{d t} 
abla f ^ {*} (g (t)), g _ {\infty} - g (t) ightangle + \left\langle 
abla f ^ {*} (g (t)), \dot {g} (t) ightangle \ &= - \left\langle  rac {d}{d t} 
abla f ^ {*} (g (t)), g _ {\infty} - g (t) ightangle \ &= \left\langle g (t) - \operatorname{proj} _ {\mathbb {B} (0, r)} (g (t)), g _ {\infty} - g (t) ightangle 	ag {3.11} \ \end{aligned}$$ where the last equality comes from (3.7). [The first cancellation uses the chain rule $ rac d{dt}f^*(g(t))=langle
abla f^*(g(t)),dot g(t)angle$, while (3.7) identifies $ rac d{dt}
abla f^*(g(t))=-(g(t)-operatorname{proj}_{mathbb B(0,r)}g(t))$.] Equivalently, $$ rac {d}{d t} D (g (t), g _ {\infty}) + \left\langle g (t) - \operatorname{proj} _ {\mathbb {B} (0, r)} (g (t)), g (t) - g _ {\infty} ightangle = 0.$$ According to the convexity of the function $\psi^{*}(\xi) =  rac{1}{2}\mathrm{dist}^{2}(\xi, \mathbb{B}(0,r))$, and $g_{\infty} \in \mathbb{B}(0,r)$ we have [The convex subgradient inequality at $g(t)$ is $psi^*(g_infty)gepsi^*(g(t))+langle
ablapsi^*(g(t)),g_infty-g(t)angle$; here $psi^*(g_infty)=0$ and $
ablapsi^*(g)=g-operatorname{proj}_{mathbb B(0,r)}g$.] $$0 \geq  rac {1}{2} \mathrm{dist} ^ {2} (g (t), \mathbb {B} (0, r)) + \left\langle g (t) - \operatorname{proj} _ {\mathbb {B} (0, r)} (g (t)), g _ {\infty} - g (t) ightangle .$$ Therefore, $$ rac {d}{d t} D (g (t), g _ {\infty}) +  rac {1}{2} \mathrm{dist} ^ {2} (g (t), \mathbb {B} (0, r)) \leq 0.$$ So, we get that $t \mapsto D(g(t), g_{\infty})$ is decreasing and $$\int_ {t _ {0}} ^ {+ \infty} \mathrm{dist} ^ {2} (
abla f (z (t)), \mathbb {B} (0, r)) d t <   + \infty . 	ag {3.12}$$ Let us now pass from the above integral estimate to a pointwise estimate. To this hand, let us take the scalar product of (3.7) with $\dot{g}(t)$. We get $$\left\langle  rac {d}{d t} \left(\partial f ^ {*} (g (t))ight), \dot {g} (t) ightangle + \left\langle g (t) - \operatorname{proj} _ {\mathbb {B} (0, r)} (g (t)), \dot {g} (t) ightangle = 0. 	ag {3.13}$$ On the one hand we have $$ rac {d}{d t} \psi^ {*} (g (t)) = \left\langle g (t) - \operatorname{proj} _ {\mathbb {B} (0, r)} (g (t)), \dot {g} (t) ightangle .$$ On the other hand $$\left\langle  rac {d}{d t} \left(\partial f ^ {*} (g (t))ight), \dot {g} (t) ightangle \geq 0.$$ Indeed, in the case where $f^{*}$ is $\mathcal{C}^2$ the above inequality is equivalent to $$\left\langle 
abla^ {2} f ^ {*} (g (t)) \dot {g} (t), \dot {g} (t) ightangle \geq 0,$$ which is satisfied by convexity of $f^{*}$. In the general case, it is obtained by exploiting the monotonicity of $\partial f^{*}$ at $g(t)$ and $g(t + h)$. Combining the above properties we get $$ rac {d}{d t} \psi^ {*} (g (t)) \leq 0. 	ag {3.14}$$ Therefore $t \mapsto \psi^{*}(g(t))$ is a decreasing function, which, according to (3.12), satisfies the following integral estimate [Since $psi^*(g)= rac12operatorname{dist}^2(g,mathbb B(0,r))$, (3.12) gives this integrability exactly.] $\int_{t_0}^{+\infty} \psi^{*}(g(t)) dt < +\infty$. We now apply Lemma 3.1 to obtain $$2 \psi^ {*} (g (t)) = \mathrm{dist} ^ {2} (
abla f (z (t)), \mathbb {B} (0, r)) = o \left( rac {1}{t}ight), 	ag {3.15}$$ and the proof is thereby completed.
items.remark: [Foundation: Foundation.Projection.BestApproximation] recall projection facts | [Note: the proof differentiates $f^*$; for nonsmooth $f^*$ this requires an absolutely-continuous subgradient selection.]

items.name: Theorem 3.3
items.statement:
Suppose that $f(x) =  rac{1}{2} \langle Ax, x angle$ where $A: \mathcal{H} 	o \mathcal{H}$ is a linear continuous operator which is symmetric and positive definite. Then for any solution trajectory $t \mapsto g(t)$ with $g(t) = 
abla f(z(t))$ of the dual version of (DRYGRAD), there is exponential convergence rate, i.e. for some $\mu > 0$ $$	ext {dist} (
abla f (z (t)), \mathbb {B} (0, r)) \leq C e ^ {- \mu t},$$ and the trajectory takes infinite time to reach this equilibria. Precisely, starting with $\| 
abla f(z(t_0))\| >r$, then for some $
u >0$ we have $$d i s t (
abla f (z (t)), \mathbb {B} (0, r)) \geq C e ^ {- 
u t}.$$ As a consequence for any trajectory z of (DRYGRAD), the equilibria is only reached after an infinite time.
items.proof:
According to $f(x) =  rac{1}{2}\langle Ax, xangle$, we have $f^{*}(x) =  rac{1}{2}\langle A^{-1}x, xangle$, where $A^{-1}$ is the inverse operator of $A$. Then, the dual version of (DRYGRAD) writes as follows $$A ^ {- 1} \dot {g} (t) + g (t) - \mathrm{proj} _ {\mathbb {B} (0, r)} (g (t)) = 0. 	ag {3.16}$$ Set briefly $h(t) =  rac{1}{2}\mathrm{dist}^2 (g(t),\mathbb{B}(0,r))$. We have $$ egin{aligned} \dot {h} (t) &= \left\langle g (t) - \operatorname{proj} _ {\mathbb {B} (0, r)} (g (t)), \dot {g} (t) ightangle \ &= - \left\langle g (t) - \operatorname{proj} _ {\mathbb {B} (0, r)} (g (t)), A (g (t)) - \operatorname{proj} _ {\mathbb {B} (0, r)} (g (t)) ightangle . \ \end{aligned}$$ Let $\mu > 0$ and $
u > 0$ such that for all $\xi \in \mathcal{H}$ $$
u \| \xi \| ^ {2} \geq \langle A \xi , \xi angle \geq \mu \| \xi \| ^ {2}.$$ Then $$\dot {h} (t) + \mu \| g (t) - \mathrm{proj} _ {\mathbb {B} (0, r)} (g (t)) \| ^ {2} \leq 0 \leq \dot {h} (t) + 
u \| g (t) - \mathrm{proj} _ {\mathbb {B} (0, r)} (g (t)) \| ^ {2}.$$ Let us now observe that $$\| g (t) - \operatorname{proj} _ {\mathbb {B} (0, r)} (g (t)) \| ^ {2} = 2 h (t).$$ Therefore we get $$\dot {h} (t) + 2 \mu h (t) \leq 0 \leq \dot {h} (t) + 2 
u h (t).$$ This immediately implies that [Integrating $dot h+2mu hle0$ gives $h(t)le h(t_0)e^{-2mu(t-t_0)}$, while $dot h+2
u hge0$ gives $h(t)ge h(t_0)e^{-2
u(t-t_0)}$; absorb the factors depending on $t_0$ into positive constants.] $$C _ {1} e ^ {- 2 
u t} \leq \mathrm{dist} ^ {2} (g (t), \mathbb {B} (0, r)) = 2 h (t) \leq C _ {2} e ^ {- 2 \mu t}.$$ and hence $$C _ {3} e ^ {- 
u t} \leq \mathrm{dist} (
abla f (z (t)), \mathbb {B} (0, r)) \leq C _ {4} e ^ {- \mu t}.$$ As a consequence, according to the definition of (DRYGRAD) we have $\dot{z}(t) 
eq 0$ for any $t \geq t_{0}$, which means that the equilibrium is reached only after an infinite time. ■
items.remark: [Prove hint: integrate the two scalar differential inequalities using positive definiteness of $A$.]

items.name: Time scaling and averaging theorem
items.statement: For the steepest-descent flow under an increasing time scale $	au$, the definitions $y(s)=z(	au(s))$ and $dot x+dot	au^{-1}(x-y)=0$ yield the weighted-average formula and the corresponding second-order inertial equation used in (4.14)--(4.15).
items.proof: Cited from: H. Attouch, R.I. Boț, D.-K. Nguyen, Fast convex optimization via time scale and averaging of the steepest descent, arXiv:2208.08260v2 [math.OC] (2022).
items.source: H. Attouch, R.I. Boț, D.-K. Nguyen, Fast convex optimization via time scale and averaging of the steepest descent, arXiv:2208.08260v2 [math.OC] (2022).
items.remark: [External: cited for the averaging representation and the time-scale derivation; the paper partially derives the needed formulas.]

items.name: Theorem 4.1
items.statement:
Time scaling and averaging of the steepest descent method with two potentials (DRYGRAD) and with time scale $	au(s) =  rac{s^2}{2(\alpha - 1)}$ give the two equivalent differential systems: (i) The couple of variables $(y, x)$ is solution of the following first-order differential system: $$\left\{  egin{aligned} \dot {y} (s) +  rac {s}{\alpha - 1} \partial \phi (\dot {y} (s)) +  rac {s}{\alpha - 1} 
abla f (y (s)) 
i 0 \ \dot {x} (s) +  rac {\alpha - 1}{s} (x (s) - y (s)) &= 0. \end{aligned} ight. 	ag {4.14}$$ (ii) $x$ is solution of the inertial system $$\ddot {x} (s) +  rac {\alpha}{s} \dot {x} (s) - (I + \partial \phi) ^ {- 1} \left[ - 
abla f \left(x (s) +  rac {s}{\alpha - 1} \dot {x} (s)ight) ight] = 0, 	ag {4.15}$$ that is $$	ext {(DRYSTAR)} \quad \ddot {x} (s) +  rac {\alpha}{s} \dot {x} (s) + 
abla f \left(x (s) +  rac {s}{\alpha - 1} \dot {x} (s)ight) - p r o j _ {\mathbb {B} (0, r)} \left(
abla f \left(x (s) +  rac {s}{\alpha - 1} \dot {x} (s)ight)ight) = 0.$$
items.remark: [Foundation: Foundation.SetValued.Basic] recall SetValuedOperator.resolvent | [Prove hint: substitute $dot	au=s/(alpha-1)$ and $(1+ddot	au)/dot	au=alpha/s$.]

items.name: Theorem 4.3
items.statement: Suppose that $f(x) = \frac{1}{2} \langle Ax, x \rangle$ where $A: \mathcal{H} \to \mathcal{H}$ is a linear continuous operator which is symmetric and positive definite. Then for any solution trajectory $x: [s_0, +\infty] \to \mathcal{H}$ of (DRYSTAR), we have the following accelerated exponentiel convergence rate: for some $\mu > 0$ $$\text {dist} \left(\nabla f \left(x (s) + \frac {s}{\alpha - 1} \dot {x} (s)\right), \mathbb {B} (0, r)\right) \leq C e ^ {- \mu s ^ {2}}.$$
items.remark: [Prove hint: compose Theorem 3.3 with $t=	au(s)$; constants absorb $2(alpha-1)$.]

items.name: Theorem 5.1
items.statement:
Let $z : [t_0, +\infty[ 	o \mathcal{H}$ be a global solution trajectory of (DRYGRAD). Then the function $g(t) := 
abla f(z(t))$ is a solution trajectory of the generalized Riemannian gradient flow $$ rac {d}{d t} \left(\partial f ^ {*} (g (t))ight) + g (t) - p r o j _ {\mathbb {B} (0, r)} (g (t)) 
i 0. 	ag {5.8}$$ Set $	au(s) =  rac{s^2}{2(\alpha - 1)}$ with $\alpha > 1$, and $v(s) = g(	au(s))$. Define $w$ as the solution of the differential equation $$\dot {w} (s) +  rac {1}{\dot {	au} (s)} (w (s) - v (s)) = 0, w i t h w (s _ {0}) = v (s _ {0}) = x _ {0}.$$ Then w satisfies the following inertial system $$	ext {(DRYSTARDE)} \quad 
abla^ {2} f ^ {*} \Big (w (s) +  rac {s}{\alpha - 1} \dot {w} (s) \Big) \Big (\ddot {w} (s) +  rac {\alpha}{s} \dot {w} (s) \Big) +

items.name: Fubini--Tonelli theorem for nonnegative integrands
items.statement: If $K(s,u)ge0$ is measurable on a product measure space, then its iterated integrals may be interchanged: $int!int K(s,u),du,ds=int!int K(s,u),ds,du$.
items.proof: Cited from: the Fubini--Tonelli inversion theorem, invoked explicitly in the proof of Theorem 4.2.
items.remark: [Prove hint: apply Tonelli to $K(s,u)=(alpha-1)s^{-alpha}u^{alpha-1}|dot y(u)|mathbf 1_{s_0le ule s}$.]

items.name: Theorem 4.2
items.statement:
Let $f: \mathcal{H} 	o \mathbb{R}$ be a convex $\mathcal{C}^1$ function, whose gradient is Lipschitz continuous on the bounded sets and such that $S = \operatorname{argmin} f 
eq \emptyset$. Suppose that $\alpha > 1$. Let $x: [s_0, +\infty[ 	o \mathcal{H}]$ be a solution trajectory of (DRYSTAR) that is $$\ddot {x} (s) +  rac {\alpha}{s} \dot {x} (s) + 
abla f \Big (x (s) +  rac {s}{\alpha - 1} \dot {x} (s) \Big) - p r o j _ {\mathbb {B} (0, r)} \left(
abla f \Big (x (s) +  rac {s}{\alpha - 1} \dot {x} (s) \Big)ight) = 0. 	ag {4.17}$$ Then: (i) $\| \dot{x}(s)\| = o\left( rac{1}{s}ight)$ as $s	o +\infty$; (ii) $\int_{s_0}^{+\infty}\| \dot{x} (s)\| ds < +\infty .$; (iii) $x(s)$ converges strongly as $s 	o +\infty$, and its limit $x_{\infty}$ satisfies $\| 
abla f(x_{\infty}) \| = r$.
items.proof:
Following [1], let us interpret the transition from $y$ to $x$ as an averaging process. Next, using techniques from integral calculus, we aim to transfer the properties of $y$, obtained from Theorem 2.1 through time scaling, to $x$. To achieve this, we recast the second equation of (4.14) as follows: $$s \dot {x} (s) + (\alpha - 1) x (s) = (\alpha - 1) y (s). \tag {4.18}$$ Then, observe that $x(s)$ can be simply written as follows (we refer to [1] for the details) [Multiply (4.18) by $s^{alpha-2}$ to obtain $ rac d{ds}(s^{alpha-1}x(s))=(alpha-1)s^{alpha-2}y(s)$; integrating from $s_0$ to $s$ and using $x(s_0)=y(s_0)$ yields (4.19).] $$x (s) = \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} y (u) d \mu_ {s} (u), \tag {4.19}$$ where $\mu_{s}$ is the positive Radon measure on $[s_0, s]$ defined by $$\mu_ {s} = \frac {s _ {0} ^ {\alpha - 1}}{s ^ {\alpha - 1}} \delta_ {s _ {0}} + (\alpha - 1) \frac {u ^ {\alpha - 2}}{s ^ {\alpha - 1}} d u,$$ where $\delta_{s_0}$ is the Dirac measure at $s_0$. We have that $\mu_{s}$ is a positive Radon measure on $[s_{0}, s]$ whose total mass is equal to 1. It is therefore a probability measure, and $\int_{s_{0}}^{s} y(u) d\mu_{s}(u)$ is obtained by averaging the trajectory $y(\cdot)$ on $[s_{0}, s]$ with respect to $\mu_{s}$. From there, we can deduce fast convergence properties for the solution trajectories of (DRYSTAR).

(i) Let us first consider the convergence rate of the velocities. According to Theorem 3.1(ii), there exists a function $\varepsilon_0(\cdot)$ with $\lim_{t\to +\infty}\varepsilon_0(t) = 0$ such that $$\| \dot {z} (t) \| = \frac {\varepsilon_ {0} (t)}{t}.$$ Therefore, $$\| \dot {z} (\tau (s)) \| = \frac {\varepsilon_ {0} (\tau (s))}{\tau (s)}. \tag {4.20}$$ Since $\dot{y}(s) = \dot{\tau}(s)\dot{z} (\tau (s))$, we deduce that $$\| \dot {y} (s) \| = \frac {\varepsilon_ {0} (\tau (s)) \dot {\tau} (s)}{\tau (s)}. \tag {4.21}$$ From $\tau(s) = \frac{s^2}{2(\alpha - 1)}$, we get $$\| \dot {y} (s) \| = \frac {\varepsilon (s)}{s}, \tag {4.22}$$ with $\varepsilon(s) = 2\varepsilon_0(\tau(s))$ which tends to zero as $s \to +\infty$. Let us now establish a similar estimate for $\|\dot{x}(s)\|$. According to the definition of $x$ $$x (s) = \frac {s _ {0} ^ {\alpha - 1}}{s ^ {\alpha - 1}} x _ {0} + \frac {\alpha - 1}{s ^ {\alpha - 1}} \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} u ^ {\alpha - 2} y (u) d u. \tag {4.23}$$ By differentiating this expression, we get $$\dot {x} (s) = - \frac {(\alpha - 1) s _ {0} ^ {\alpha - 1}}{s ^ {\alpha}} x _ {0} - \frac {(\alpha - 1) ^ {2}}{s ^ {\alpha}} \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} u ^ {\alpha - 2} y (u) d u + (\alpha - 1) \frac {1}{s} y (s). \tag {4.24}$$ Let us reformulate this expression in terms of $\dot{y}(s)$, which is the quantity whose speed of convergence is known by (4.22). Indeed, by integration by parts we have $$\int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} u ^ {\alpha - 1} \dot {y} (u) d u = s ^ {\alpha - 1} y (s) - s _ {0} ^ {\alpha - 1} y (s _ {0}) - (\alpha - 1) \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} u ^ {\alpha - 2} y (u) d u.$$ After multiplication of the above expression by $\frac{\alpha-1}{s^{\alpha}}$, and according to $y(s_{0})=x_{0}$, we get $$\frac {\alpha - 1}{s ^ {\alpha}} \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} u ^ {\alpha - 1} \dot {y} (u) d u = (\alpha - 1) \frac {1}{s} y (s) - \frac {(\alpha - 1) s _ {0} ^ {\alpha - 1}}{s ^ {\alpha}} x _ {0} - \frac {(\alpha - 1) ^ {2}}{s ^ {\alpha}} \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} u ^ {\alpha - 2} y (u) d u. \tag {4.25}$$ Comparing (4.24) and (4.25) we get $$\dot {x} (s) = \frac {\alpha - 1}{s ^ {\alpha}} \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} u ^ {\alpha - 1} \dot {y} (u) d u. \tag {4.26}$$ After multiplication of (4.26) by $s$, and according to (4.22), we obtain successively $$s \dot {x} (s) = \frac {\alpha - 1}{s ^ {\alpha - 1}} \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} u ^ {\alpha - 2} u \dot {y} (u) d u$$ $$s \| \dot {x} (s) \| \leq \frac {\alpha - 1}{s ^ {\alpha - 1}} \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} u ^ {\alpha - 2} \varepsilon (u) d u.$$ Since $\varepsilon(s)$ tends to zero as $s \to +\infty$, by applying Lemma A.1 we obtain $\lim_{s \to +\infty} \|s\dot{x}(s)\| = 0$.

(ii) According to Theorem 2.1 (ii), we have $$\int_ {t _ {0}} ^ {+ \infty} \| \dot {z} (t) \| d t <   + \infty$$ i.e., the trajectory $z(\cdot)$ has a finite length. This property being invariant by change of time variable, we have that $$\int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {+ \infty} \| \dot {y} (s) \| d s <   + \infty .$$ According to (4.26) we have that $$\| \dot {x} (s) \| \leq \frac {\alpha - 1}{s ^ {\alpha}} \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} u ^ {\alpha - 1} \| \dot {y} (u) \| d u. \tag {4.27}$$ Therefore $$\begin{aligned} \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {+ \infty} \| \dot {x} (s) \| d s &\leq \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {+ \infty} \left(\frac {\alpha - 1}{s ^ {\alpha}} \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} u ^ {\alpha - 1} \| \dot {y} (u) \| d u\right) d s (4.28) \\ &= \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {+ \infty} \| \dot {y} (u) \| d u <   + \infty (4.29) \\ \end{aligned}$$ where the last equality follows from a simple calculus using the Fubini--Tonelli inversion theorem for the multiple integral of a nonnegative function. [Indeed, Tonelli changes the left side into $int_{s_0}^infty u^{alpha-1}|dot y(u)|(alpha-1)int_u^infty s^{-alpha}ds,du=int_{s_0}^infty|dot y(u)|du$.]

(iii) Therefore, we have that the trajectory $x(\cdot)$ converges strongly to some $x_{\infty}$. Let us verify that $$\lim _ {t \to + \infty} z (t) = \lim _ {s \to + \infty} y (s) = \lim _ {s \to + \infty} x (s).$$ Indeed, the first equality is an immediate consequence of $y(s) = z(\tau(s))$ and $\tau(s) \to +\infty$ as $s \to +\infty$. The second equality follows again from the averaging property, and from the general property which says that convergence entails ergodic convergence. Let us make this precise. By definition of $x(s)$ $$x (s) = \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} y (u) d \mu_ {s} (u) = \frac {s _ {0} ^ {\alpha - 1}}{s ^ {\alpha - 1}} y (s _ {0}) + \frac {\alpha - 1}{s ^ {\alpha - 1}} \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} u ^ {\alpha - 2} y (u) d u.$$ Let $y_{\infty} = \lim_{s \to +\infty} y(s)$. Since $\mu_s$ is a probability measure $$x (s) - y _ {\infty} = \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} (y (u) - y _ {\infty}) d \mu_ {s} (u) = \frac {s _ {0} ^ {\alpha - 1}}{s ^ {\alpha - 1}} (y (s _ {0}) - y _ {\infty}) + \frac {\alpha - 1}{s ^ {\alpha - 1}} \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} u ^ {\alpha - 2} (y (u) - y _ {\infty}) d u.$$ Therefore $$\| x (s) - y _ {\infty} \| \leq \frac {s _ {0} ^ {\alpha - 1}}{s ^ {\alpha - 1}} \| y (s _ {0}) - y _ {\infty} \| + \frac {\alpha - 1}{s ^ {\alpha - 1}} \int_ {s _ {0}} ^ {s} u ^ {\alpha - 2} \| y (u) - y _ {\infty} \| d u.$$ The equality $\lim_{s\to +\infty}y(s) = \lim_{s\to +\infty}x(s)$ follows from a direct application of Lemma A.1. [Apply Lemma A.1 to $a(u)=|y(u)-y_infty|$, which is nonnegative and tends to $0$; the atomic coefficient $s_0^{alpha-1}/s^{alpha-1}$ also tends to $0$.] According to Theorem 2.1 (iii) we thus have that $x(s)$ converges strongly as $s\to +\infty$, and its limit $x_{\infty}$ satisfies $$\| \nabla f (x _ {\infty}) \| = r,$$ which completes the proof. ■
items.remark: [Prove hint: solve the linear ODE for $x$, then use Tonelli on the nonnegative kernel.]

items.name: Remark 4.1
items.statement: As a general rule, the trajectories $z(\cdot)$ and $y(\cdot)$ ultimately reach the same equilibrium in finite time. As a result, for some finite time $\bar{s}$, we can conclude that $y(\bar{s}) = x_{\infty}$. Using the average formula in Eq. (4.23), we can compute that for all $s \geq \bar{s}$, the following expression holds: $$x (s) = x _ {\infty} + \frac {C}{S ^ {\alpha - 1}}. \tag {4.30}$$ Thus, finite-time stabilization is no longer valid for $x(\cdot)$, but it is nearly true when $\alpha$ is large.
items.remark: [Note: equation (4.30) writes $S$ where the time variable should likely be $s$; retain source notation.]

items.name: Classical gradient-flow value rate
items.statement:
For a convex differentiable function with an attained infimum, the classical gradient flow $dot y+
abla f(y)=0$ satisfies $f(y(s))-inf f=o(1/s)$ under the regularity assumptions invoked in Appendix A.
items.proof: Cited from: the classical convergence property of the classical descent method, invoked in the proof of Theorem A.1; no bibliographic source is supplied in the paper.
items.remark: [Note: formalization needs the exact hypotheses and a source; the paper states this result without them.]

items.name: Theorem A.1
items.statement: Let $z : [t_{0}, +\infty] \to H$ be a global solution trajectory of (DRYGRAD). Then, $t \mapsto f(z(t))$ is a decreasing function, and the following convergence rate is satisfied: as $t \to +\infty$ $$f (z (t)) - f _ {*} = o \left(\frac {1}{\ln t}\right),$$ where $f_{*} = \inf \{f(z(t)): t \geq t_{0}\}$.
items.proof:
According to (2.3), we have $$\| \dot {z} (t) \| ^ {2} +  rac {d}{d t} f (z (t)) \leq 0. 	ag {A.1}$$ So $ rac{d}{dt} f(z(t)) \leq 0$, which implies that (DRYGRAD) is a descent method. We analyze the case where convergence holds in infinite time. The case of finite convergence requires a different analysis. So let us introduce $$f _ {*} = \inf \left\{f (z (t)): t \geq t _ {0} ight\}.$$ So we have $f(z(t)) \downarrow f_{*}$ as $t ightarrow +\infty$. Let us rewrite (DRYGRAD) as the non-autonomous gradient system $$\dot {z} (t) + \gamma (t) 
abla f (z (t)) = 0, 	ag {A.2}$$ where $$\gamma (t) =  rac {1}{1 +  rac {r}{\| \dot {z} (t) \|}} =  rac {\| \dot {z} (t) \|}{r + \| \dot {z} (t) \|}.$$ We have already proved that $\| \dot{z}(t)\| = o\left( rac{1}{t}ight)$. Therefore, given $\epsilon >0$, for $t$ sufficiently large $$\gamma (t) =  rac {\| \dot {z} (t) \|}{r + \| \dot {z} (t) \|} \leq  rac {\epsilon}{t}.$$ Let us now interpret (A.2) as a time rescaled steepest descent. Set $t = 	heta(s)$ where $	heta$ is an increasing function that will be fixed later. Set $y(s) = z(	heta(s))$. We have $$\dot {y} (s) + \gamma (	heta (s)) \dot {	heta} (s) 
abla f (y (s)) = 0. 	ag {A.3}$$ Take $	heta$ such that $$\gamma (	heta (s)) \dot {	heta} (s) = 1.$$ Let us integrate this differential equation, and introduce $\Gamma = \int \gamma$ a primitive of $\gamma$. Therefore $\Gamma' = \gamma \geq 0$ which implies that $\Gamma$ is an increasing function. We thus have $$ rac {d}{d s} \Gamma (	heta (s)) = 1,$$ which gives $$\Gamma (	heta (s)) = s.$$ So, $	heta$ is the inverse function of $\Gamma$ , which implies that it is an increasing function. A careful inspection shows that $\lim_{t	o +\infty}\Gamma (t) = \Gamma_{\infty} < +\infty$ , because $x(\cdot)$ has finite length. So the time scaling is between $t\in [s_0, + \infty[$ and $s = 	heta^{-1}(t) = \Gamma (t)\in [s_0,\Gamma_\infty[$ . Since $\gamma (t)\leq  rac{\epsilon}{t}$ , and $\Gamma' = \gamma$ , we have $$\Gamma (s) \leq \epsilon \ln (s).$$ Therefore $$s = \Gamma (	heta (s)) \leq \epsilon \ln (	heta (s)),$$ which gives $$	heta (s) \geq \exp ( rac {1}{\epsilon} s).$$ On the other hand, according to a classical convergence property of the classical descent method $$\dot {y} (s) + 
abla f (y (s)) = 0, 	ag {A.4}$$ we have $$f (y (s)) - f _ {*} \leq f (y (s)) - \inf f = o \left( rac {1}{s}ight).$$ Since $y(s) = z(	heta(s))$, we get $$f (z (	heta (s))) - f _ {*} = o \left( rac {1}{s}ight).$$ Since for $z$, we have a descent method and $	heta(s) \geq \exp( rac{1}{\epsilon}s)$ we deduce that [Because $	heta(s)ge e^{s/epsilon}$ and $f(z(cdot))$ is nonincreasing, $f(z(e^{s/epsilon}))ge f(z(	heta(s)))$; thus the displayed inequality has the direction written in the source reversed. [TODO: verify] the final rate cannot be concluded from this comparison without an additional argument.] $$f (z (\exp ( rac {1}{\epsilon} s))) - f _ {*} \leq f (z (	heta (s))) - f _ {*} = o \left( rac {1}{s}ight).$$ This gives $$f (z (t)) - f _ {*} = o \left( rac {1}{\ln t}ight),$$ which completes the proof. ■
items.remark: [Note: the proof’s time variable has a finite upper endpoint when $intgamma<infty$; the invoked gradient-flow rate needs exact hypotheses and a careful reparameterization.]

items.name: Gorni conjugation and second-order expansion result
items.statement: If a proper lower-semicontinuous convex $f:mathbb R^n	omathbb Rcup{+infty}$ has $f(x)= rac12langle Ax,xangle+o(|x|^2)$ at $0$, with $A$ symmetric positive definite, then $f^*(y)= rac12langle A^{-1}y,yangle+o(|y|^2)$ at $0$.
items.proof: Cited from: G. Gorni, Conjugation and second-order properties of convex functions, J. Math. Anal. Appl. 158 (1991) 293--315.
items.source: G. Gorni, Conjugation and second-order properties of convex functions, J. Math. Anal. Appl. 158 (1991) 293--315.
items.remark: [External: used only in Remark 3.1.]

items.name: Remark 3.1
items.statement:
Let $f: \mathbb{R}^n 	o \mathbb{R} \cup +\infty$ be a convex, proper and lower semicontinuous function. It is known that the Legendre-Fenchel conjugate $f^*$ associated with $f$ is related to the subdifferential of $f$ as follows: $$ egin{aligned} y &\in \partial f (x) \iff f (x) + f ^ {*} (y) = \langle y, x angle \ \Longleftrightarrow x &\in \partial f ^ {*} (y). \ \end{aligned}$$ Thus, the inverse of the subdifferential of $f$, $\partial f$, as a set-valued operator is $\partial f^*$, i.e. $\partial f^* = (\partial f)^{-1}$. If $f:\mathbb{R}^n	o \mathbb{R}$ is convex and of class $\mathcal{C}^1$, then $$y \in \partial f (x) \iff y = 
abla f (x).$$ Suppose that $
abla f: \mathbb{R}^n 	o \mathbb{R}^n$ is nonsingular with a continuous inverse. Then $f^*$ is also of class $\mathcal{C}^1$ and $$
abla f ^ {*} = \left(
abla fight) ^ {- 1}.$$ Furthermore, if $f$ is convex and twice continuously differentiable, i.e. $f$ is of class $\mathcal{C}^2$, with a nonsingular Hessian matrix $
abla^2 f(x)$ at every point $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, then by using the inverse function theorem, we have $$\left(
abla^ {2} f (x)ight) ^ {- 1} = 
abla^ {2} f ^ {*} (y), 	ext {with} y = 
abla f (x).$$ We note that this formula can be rewritten in terms of associated quadratic forms as follows $$y \in \partial f (x) \Longrightarrow Q _ {f ^ {*}} (y) = \left(Q _ {f} (x)ight) ^ {*},$$ where $Q_{f}(x)= rac{1}{2}\langle
abla^{2}f(x)z,zangle$ is the associated quadratic form with the Hessian matrix of f. The following result linking conjugation and second-order properties of convex functions was proved by G. Gorni in [44]. Let $f: \mathbb{R}^n 	o \mathbb{R} \cup +\infty$ be a convex, proper and lower semicontinuous function. If $f$ has a second-order Taylor expansion at the origin $$f (x) =  rac {1}{2} \langle A x, x angle + o (\| x \| ^ {2}) 	ext {   as   } x 	o 0,$$ with A symmetric and positive definite, then $f^{*}$ has also a second-order Taylor expansion at the origin, which is given by $$f ^ {*} (y) =  rac {1}{2} \langle A ^ {- 1} y, y angle + o (\| y \| ^ {2}) 	ext {as} y 	o 0.$
